questions.question: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Test
questions.direct_answer: A **unit test** checks a single class in isolation using **mocks** and never starts Spring. An **integration test** boots part or all of the Spring context and verifies real **wiring** between components. Unit tests run in milliseconds with Mockito; integration tests use **@SpringBootTest** or slice annotations like **@WebMvcTest**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the testing pyramid and knows when each test type is appropriate in a Spring Boot project.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for service tests and calling them unit tests, or thinking unit tests always require Spring context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the testing pyramid by name and explain the speed-confidence trade-off: unit tests are 100x faster but integration tests catch wiring bugs that mocks can't simulate.

sections.title: Two Different Testing Approaches
sections.content:
Unit tests and integration tests serve different purposes in a Spring Boot application. A **unit test** isolates a single class—usually a service or utility—and replaces all dependencies with **mocks** using Mockito.

It runs in pure Java without starting the Spring container, testing business logic in microseconds. An **integration test** starts the Spring **application context** (or a slice of it) and verifies that real beans wire together correctly. It tests the **interaction** between components: does the controller call the service? Does the service save to the real repository? Think of unit tests as checking each gear in isolation, while integration tests spin multiple gears together to verify the mechanism works. Unit tests dominate in number because they're fast; integration tests are fewer but catch wiring mistakes that mocks can't simulate.

sections.title: Unit vs Integration at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Unit test|~One class, mocked deps|no Spring context|Mockito @Mock|runs in milliseconds
blue|Integration test|~Real beans wired|@SpringBootTest or slice|hits real DB or HTTP|2-5s startup
amber|Testing pyramid|~Many fast, few slow|70-80% unit|15-20% integration|5-10% end-to-end
rose|Common trap|~@SpringBootTest everywhere|turns units into slow tests|suite crawls|use mocks for logic

sections.title: Unit Test vs Integration Test
sections.content:
| Aspect | Unit Test | Integration Test |
|---|---|---|
| Spring context | No context loaded | Full or sliced context loaded |
| Dependencies | Mocked with Mockito | Real Spring beans injected |
| Speed | Milliseconds per test | 2-5 seconds startup plus execution |
| Annotations | @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) | @SpringBootTest or slice annotations |
| What it tests | Single class business logic | Component wiring and interactions |

sections.title: Unit Test — Isolated With Mocks
Integration Test — Real Wiring
When to Use Each Test Type
sections.content:
Use **unit tests** for service classes with business logic, utility methods, validators, and mappers. They form the base of your testing pyramid—write hundreds of them because they run in under 10ms each. A ProductService calculating discounts? Unit test with a mocked ProductRepository.

Use **integration tests** when you need to verify Spring wiring: a REST controller calling a service calling a repository, or a scheduled job triggering multiple beans. Write these for critical paths like user registration or payment processing where real database transactions matter. Keep integration tests under 20% of your total test count because each one costs 3-5 seconds of context startup, multiplying quickly across a large test suite.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unit test** — tests one class in isolation with mocked dependencies, no Spring context, runs in milliseconds.
- **Integration test** — loads the Spring context (full or slice), tests real bean wiring, takes 2-5 seconds to start.
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** — the JUnit 5 annotation for unit tests using Mockito mocks.
- **@SpringBootTest** — starts the full application context for integration tests, slow but comprehensive.
- **Testing pyramid** — many unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, minimal end-to-end tests on top.
- **Speed difference** — unit tests are 100-1000x faster because they skip context startup and I/O.
- **Trade-off** — unit tests are fast but can't catch wiring bugs; integration tests are slow but verify real interactions.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A unit test checks a single class in isolation using mocks. It doesn't start the Spring container. You'd use Mockito to mock dependencies like repositories or external services, then test just the business logic. For example, testing a service method that calculates order totals—you'd mock the repository and verify the calculation logic. An integration test is different. It starts the Spring context, either fully with the SpringBootTest annotation or partially with slice annotations like WebMvcTest. It tests how real beans wire together. So you'd write an integration test to verify that a controller actually calls the service, and the service actually saves to the database. The key difference is speed. Unit tests run in milliseconds because there's no context startup. Integration tests take three to five seconds just to boot Spring before running any assertions. In a real project, you'd want maybe eighty percent unit tests and twenty percent integration tests. That's the testing pyramid—lots of fast tests at the base, fewer slow tests higher up. The mistake freshers make is putting the SpringBootTest annotation on every test. That turns everything into an integration test, and your test suite becomes painfully slow.

questions.question: Why are unit tests faster than integration tests in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Why Unit Tests Are Faster
questions.direct_answer: Unit tests have **no Spring context startup** and **no I/O** — they run pure Java logic against in-memory mocks in milliseconds. Integration tests must start the **application context** (2-5 seconds) and often add database or network calls, so the cost multiplies across the suite.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what actually makes tests slow—context startup, I/O, network—not just code complexity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking unit tests are faster simply because they test less code or have fewer assertions.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Quantify the difference: mention that Spring context startup can take 3-5 seconds and that this cost multiplies across hundreds of tests in a real project, turning a 10-second unit test suite into a 30-minute integration test suite.

sections.title: What Makes Tests Slow
sections.content:
The speed difference between unit and integration tests comes down to three factors: **context startup**, **I/O operations**, and **dependency complexity**. A unit test in Spring Boot is just plain Java—JUnit instantiates your service class, Mockito injects mock objects, and your test runs method calls in RAM.

Total time: 2-10 milliseconds. An integration test, on the other hand, must start the **Spring application context**: scanning classpath for beans, autowiring dependencies, initializing connection pools, loading configuration. This startup alone takes 2-5 seconds for a typical Spring Boot app. Then if your test hits a database (even H2 in-memory), each query adds 5-50ms. If it calls a REST endpoint with MockMvc, add 10-20ms for HTTP serialization. Multiply these costs across 200 tests, and you've turned a 2-second unit test suite into a 15-minute integration test suite. The analogy: unit tests are calculator keystrokes; integration tests are booting a laptop before every calculation.

sections.title: Where the Time Goes
sections.content:
rose|Context startup|~The big cost|scan beans, autowire|init pools, read config|2-5s before any assert
amber|I/O per test|~Adds up fast|DB query 5-50ms|HTTP serialize 10-20ms|network latency
emerald|Unit test path|~Pure Java in RAM|JUnit plus Mockito mocks|no context, no I/O|2-10ms total
blue|Cumulative|~Multiplied across suite|200 integration is minutes|200 unit is seconds|measure per test

sections.title: Speed Comparison Example
When Speed Matters
sections.content:
Speed matters most during **local development**. Developers run tests hundreds of times per day while coding. If each test run takes 5 minutes instead of 5 seconds, you lose an hour daily waiting.

Use unit tests for rapid feedback loops: test-driven development, refactoring, debugging edge cases. In **CI/CD pipelines**, a slow test suite blocks deployments. A 30-minute integration test suite means every pull request waits half an hour for feedback, killing team velocity.

Use integration tests strategically: critical user flows, database migrations, API contract tests.

Avoid integration tests for simple logic like validators or formatters—those should be unit tested. On a team of 10 developers making 50 commits per day, shaving 2 minutes off test suite time saves 100 minutes of CI compute daily. That's real cost savings and faster iterations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking less code equals faster tests**: A unit test with 100 assertions runs faster than an integration test with 1 assertion if the integration test starts Spring. Speed comes from avoiding I/O, not reducing logic.
- **Not measuring test time**: Freshers don't notice when tests slow down. Run your test suite with verbose output—JUnit reports time per test. If any test takes over 500ms, investigate.
- **Using real databases in integration tests without cleanup**: Each test leaves data, slowing down subsequent tests as table scans grow. Use @Transactional or @DirtiesContext to reset state, or switch to Testcontainers for isolation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Context startup cost** — the Spring Boot context takes 2-5 seconds to initialize in integration tests.
- **I/O operations** — database queries add 5-50ms each; REST calls add 10-20ms for serialization.
- **Memory-only execution** — unit tests run pure Java in RAM with mocked dependencies, no external I/O.
- **Cumulative impact** — 200 integration tests x 3 seconds is 10 minutes; 200 unit tests x 5ms is 1 second.
- **CI/CD bottleneck** — slow suites delay deployments and waste compute in build pipelines.
- **Pyramid ratio** — aim for 70-80% unit tests to keep overall suite time under 2 minutes.
- **Measurement** — use JUnit's time reporting to find slow tests and refactor them to unit tests where possible.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Unit tests are faster because they skip two expensive operations: starting Spring and doing input-output. When you run a unit test, JUnit just creates your service class and injects Mockito mocks. Everything runs in memory. That's why a unit test finishes in five or ten milliseconds. Integration tests have to start the Spring application context first. Spring scans for beans, wires dependencies, sets up connection pools. That startup alone takes three to five seconds. Then if your test hits a database, even an in-memory one like H2, each query adds another ten to fifty milliseconds. In a real project, this difference multiplies. If you have two hundred tests and they're all integration tests, you're waiting ten to fifteen minutes. If they're unit tests, you're done in under ten seconds. That's a huge deal during development. You'd run tests constantly while coding, so fast feedback is critical. The mistake freshers make is not measuring test time. They write the SpringBootTest annotation everywhere and wonder why tests feel slow. Always check the test report—if anything takes over half a second, ask yourself if it really needs the full Spring context.

questions.question: In a Spring Boot project, what does a typical unit test look like compared to an integration test?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Test Structure
questions.direct_answer: A **unit test** uses `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` with `@Mock` for dependencies and tests one class directly. An **integration test** uses `@SpringBootTest` to load the context and tests real beans wired together, usually with `@Autowired` to inject actual components.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can write or recognize both test types and knows the annotation differences from memory.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest on a service unit test, wasting context startup time and calling it a unit test.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both test structures from memory with correct imports and explain why each annotation is chosen for its purpose—demonstrate you've written both types in real projects.

sections.title: Structural Differences in Test Classes
sections.content:
Unit tests and integration tests have distinct code structures that reflect their different purposes. A **unit test** extends JUnit with Mockito, using `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` at the class level.

Dependencies are marked with `@Mock`, and the class under test uses `@InjectMocks` to receive those mocks automatically. You call methods directly on the test subject and verify interactions with `verify()`. No Spring annotations appear—it's pure JUnit and Mockito. An **integration test** uses `@SpringBootTest` to load the application context. Real beans are injected with `@Autowired`, not mocked. You're testing the actual wiring: does the controller call the service? Does the service commit to the database? The test class reads like production code—calling HTTP endpoints with MockMvc or invoking service methods that trigger real repository saves. The structure signals intent: unit tests isolate, integration tests connect.

sections.title: Read the Annotations to Tell Them Apart
sections.content:
emerald|Unit shape|~Mockito wiring|@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension)|@Mock plus @InjectMocks|verify() on mocks
blue|Integration shape|~Spring wiring|@SpringBootTest|@Autowired real beans|MockMvc or TestRestTemplate
amber|Imports tell|~Quick recognition|Mockito plus JUnit is unit|Spring Test is integration|read it in review
rose|Trap|~@SpringBootTest on a service|4s startup for logic|called integration|prefer Mockito here

sections.title: Unit Test vs Integration Test Structure
sections.content:
| Element | Unit Test | Integration Test |
|---|---|---|
| Class annotation | @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) | @SpringBootTest |
| Dependency injection | @Mock and @InjectMocks | @Autowired for real beans |
| Setup | Manual or @BeforeEach | Spring context auto-wires beans |
| Imports | Mockito, JUnit only | Spring Test, JUnit, often MockMvc |
| Assertions | verify() for mock calls | assertEquals on real data or HTTP responses |

sections.title: Unit Test Structure — Mockito Only
Integration Test Structure — Real Context
When Each Structure Fits
sections.content:
Use the **unit test structure** for service classes, validators, mappers, and utility methods. If the class has constructor-injected dependencies and business logic, a unit test with mocked dependencies is the right fit. Example: an OrderService that calculates totals—mock the OrderRepository and test discount logic.

Use the **integration test structure** when you need to verify bean wiring or external I/O. A REST controller test needs MockMvc to send HTTP requests and verify JSON responses. A repository test needs @DataJpaTest to check if your custom query works against a real database schema. An end-to-end test needs @SpringBootTest with a running server to test the full request lifecycle from controller through service to database. The structure you choose broadcasts what you're testing: logic in isolation or components in concert.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** — the JUnit 5 annotation that enables Mockito's @Mock and @InjectMocks in unit tests.
- **@Mock** — creates a mock for a dependency, isolating the class under test.
- **@InjectMocks** — injects all @Mock objects into the test subject's constructor or fields.
- **@SpringBootTest** — loads the full context to test real component wiring in integration tests.
- **@Autowired** — injects real Spring beans from the loaded context, not mocks.
- **MockMvc** — simulates HTTP requests to controllers without starting a real server.
- **Slice annotations** — @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest load only part of the context, faster than @SpringBootTest for focused tests.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A typical unit test starts with the ExtendWith annotation taking MockitoExtension dot class at the top. That enables Mockito in JUnit 5. Then you'd mark your dependencies with the Mock annotation, like your repository or external service. The class you're testing gets the InjectMocks annotation so Mockito injects those mocks for you. In the test method, you'd use when then-return to stub behaviour, call your service method, and then assert the result or verify the mock was called. No Spring involved—just pure Java and mocks. An integration test looks different. You'd use the SpringBootTest annotation at the class level. That boots the actual Spring context. Then you'd use the Autowired annotation to inject real beans, like your controller or service. For a REST API test, you'd also inject MockMvc to simulate HTTP requests. Your test methods call the real service, which calls the real repository, which hits a real database—usually H2 in memory for tests. You'd assert on the actual data saved or the JSON response. The key visual difference is the annotations. If you see Mock and InjectMocks, it's a unit test. If you see SpringBootTest and Autowired, it's integration. That's how you'd recognise them in a code review too.

questions.question: What is the testing pyramid and how does it apply to Spring Boot applications?
questions.title: Testing Pyramid in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The **testing pyramid** recommends many fast **unit tests** at the base, fewer **integration tests** in the middle, and very few slow **end-to-end tests** at the top. In Spring Boot that means mostly service unit tests with mocked repositories, some slice tests for controllers and data layers, and minimal full **@SpringBootTest** tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has a structured view of testing strategy, not just knowledge of individual annotations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing integration tests for everything or ignoring unit tests entirely, creating an inverted pyramid that makes the test suite unbearably slow.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map each Spring testing annotation to its pyramid layer and explain the trade-off: more tests at the base means faster feedback loops, but you need some higher-layer tests to catch real-world integration bugs.

sections.title: The Testing Pyramid Strategy
sections.content:
The **testing pyramid** is a testing strategy that optimizes for speed and confidence. Visualize a pyramid: the wide base holds hundreds of **unit tests** that run in milliseconds and test individual classes in isolation.

The middle layer contains dozens of **integration tests** that verify components work together, taking seconds to run. The narrow top has a handful of **end-to-end tests** that exercise the full system, taking minutes. The pyramid shape reflects both quantity and speed: more tests at lower layers where they're cheap, fewer at higher layers where they're expensive. In a Spring Boot application, this translates to mostly service unit tests with mocked repositories (base), some slice tests using @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest (middle), and minimal @SpringBootTest with a running server (top). The pyramid keeps test suites fast while still catching bugs at every integration level. An **inverted pyramid**—mostly E2E tests, few unit tests—creates a brittle, slow test suite that blocks deployments.

sections.title: The Three Layers Mapped to Spring
sections.content:
emerald|Base|~Unit tests|70-80% of suite|mocked dependencies|milliseconds each
blue|Middle|~Slice tests|15-20% of suite|@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest|seconds each
rose|Top|~End-to-end|5-10% of suite|@SpringBootTest plus server|slowest, fewest
amber|Inverted is bad|~Mostly E2E|slow and brittle|blocks deployments|avoid this shape

sections.title: Pyramid Layers in Spring Boot
Applying the Pyramid to Spring Boot Projects
sections.content:
Follow this distribution: **70-80% unit tests** at the base. Test every service class, every utility, every validator with mocked dependencies. Each test runs in 5-10ms. A 400-test suite finishes in 3 seconds. **15-20% integration tests** in the middle.

Use @WebMvcTest for REST controllers to test request mapping and validation.

Use @DataJpaTest for repositories to verify custom queries against a real schema. These take 1-3 seconds each due to partial context loading. **5-10% end-to-end tests** at the top.

Use @SpringBootTest with a running server for critical user journeys: user registration, payment processing, admin workflows. These take 5-10 seconds each. Run the full suite in under 2 minutes even with 500 tests. In a real project, resist the temptation to write integration tests first because they 'feel more real.' Start with unit tests for fast feedback, add slice tests for controllers and repositories, and reserve full E2E tests for happy paths that cross multiple bounded contexts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inverted pyramid**: Writing mostly integration or E2E tests because 'they test more code.' This creates a slow, fragile suite. A 100-test suite of @SpringBootTest tests takes 8 minutes to run, killing local development flow.
- **Ignoring unit tests entirely**: Freshers skip unit tests and jump straight to integration tests because they don't understand mocking. They end up with slow tests and poor coverage of edge cases.
- **Not using slice annotations**: Using @SpringBootTest when @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest would load only the needed slice, cutting test time from 5 seconds to 1 second.
- **Testing implementation details**: Writing unit tests that verify internal method calls instead of outputs, making tests brittle and hard to refactor.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pyramid shape** — a wide base of unit tests, a narrow middle of integration tests, a tiny top of E2E tests.
- **Speed gradient** — unit tests run in milliseconds, integration tests in seconds, E2E tests in minutes.
- **Base layer** — service unit tests with @Mock dependencies, testing logic in isolation.
- **Middle layer** — slice tests with @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest, loading only part of the context.
- **Top layer** — full @SpringBootTest tests with a running server, for critical end-to-end flows.
- **Ratio target** — aim for 70-80% unit, 15-20% integration, 5-10% E2E.
- **Inverted anti-pattern** — mostly E2E tests creates slow, brittle suites that block deployments.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The testing pyramid is a strategy for balancing speed and confidence. Picture a pyramid with three layers. The wide base holds lots of unit tests—maybe seventy or eighty percent of your total tests. These run in milliseconds because they're just Java logic with mocked dependencies. In Spring Boot, that's your service classes tested with Mockito. No Spring context. The middle layer has fewer integration tests, maybe fifteen or twenty percent. These use slice annotations like WebMvcTest or DataJpaTest to load only part of the Spring context. You'd test a controller with MockMvc or a repository with a real database schema. Each takes one to three seconds. The narrow top has just a few end-to-end tests, maybe five or ten percent. These use the SpringBootTest annotation with a running server to test critical flows from API to database. Each takes five to ten seconds. The pyramid shape keeps your test suite fast. If you have five hundred tests and follow the pyramid, you'd run them all in under two minutes. The mistake freshers make is inverting the pyramid—writing mostly full-context tests because they seem easier or more realistic. That creates a thirty-minute test suite nobody wants to run. Always start with unit tests for the base, add slice tests for the layers, and reserve full integration tests for the critical paths.

questions.question: Should you test your Spring service layer with unit tests or integration tests? Why?
questions.title: Testing the Service Layer
questions.direct_answer: Test service-layer **business logic with unit tests** using mocked repositories — it's pure Java and needs no context. Reach for integration tests only to verify **real database transactions**, complex queries, or cross-service wiring. Unit tests are roughly 100x faster and pinpoint logic bugs precisely.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment about which test type belongs at which layer of a Spring Boot application.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every service test, making the suite very slow without gaining meaningful coverage.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the clear separation: service = unit test with mocked repo, controller = @WebMvcTest, repository = @DataJpaTest, only use @SpringBootTest for cross-layer flows.

sections.title: Service Layer Testing Strategy
sections.content:
The service layer contains your **business logic**—validation, calculations, orchestration of repository calls, and decision-making. This logic is **pure Java** and doesn't require Spring context, databases, or HTTP layers to verify. **Unit tests** with mocked dependencies are the right tool here because they isolate the logic you actually wrote from infrastructure.

Think of it like testing a calculator: you don't need to boot an entire application to verify that 2 + 2 returns 4. Integration tests should be reserved for proving that your **actual database queries work** or that **multiple Spring beans wire together correctly**—scenarios where mocks can't validate the real behavior. A typical Spring Boot project should have 80% unit tests (fast, isolated) and 20% integration tests (slow, comprehensive).

sections.title: Match the Layer to the Test
sections.content:
emerald|Service layer|~Pure business logic|unit test with mocks|mock the repository|fast and precise
blue|Repository layer|~Real queries|@DataJpaTest|in-memory H2|verify the JPQL
amber|Controller layer|~HTTP mapping|@WebMvcTest plus MockMvc|mock the service|status and JSON
rose|Cross-layer flow|~End-to-end only|@SpringBootTest|real transactions|reserve for critical paths

sections.title: Unit Testing a Service with Mocked Repository
When to Use Each Test Type
sections.content:
Use **unit tests** for service layer methods that transform data, validate input, calculate results, or orchestrate repository calls—anything that's pure logic. Example: testing that a pricing service applies the correct discount based on customer tier.

Use **integration tests** when you need to verify that a custom JPQL query returns the right rows, that @Transactional rollback works correctly, or that multiple services interact properly through Spring's dependency injection. Example: testing that an order creation flow correctly updates inventory, creates audit logs, and commits the transaction atomically. Reserve @SpringBootTest for **end-to-end scenarios** like "POST /orders should return 201 and persist to database."

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for service tests**: Freshers add @SpringBootTest to every test class, causing the full Spring context to load for simple business logic checks. This makes tests 50-100x slower and hides what you're actually testing.
- **Not mocking repository dependencies**: Writing service tests that call real repositories without understanding that you're no longer testing service logic—you're testing JPA and database behavior.
- **Testing getter/setter logic**: Writing unit tests that verify a record's fields are set correctly, which adds no value since the compiler already guarantees this.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unit test scope** — tests a single class in isolation with mocked dependencies, verifying business logic only.
- **Integration test scope** — tests multiple components together with real infrastructure like databases or HTTP clients.
- **Speed difference** — unit tests run in milliseconds; integration tests take seconds due to context startup and I/O.
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** — the correct annotation for unit tests; no Spring context loads.
- **@SpringBootTest overhead** — loads all beans, connects to databases, reads configuration; unnecessary for pure logic.
- **Pyramid principle** — 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% end-to-end in a production Spring Boot app.
- **Feedback loop** — unit tests fail instantly when logic breaks; integration tests fail when wiring or infrastructure breaks.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You should test your service layer with unit tests, not integration tests. The service layer contains business logic—things like validation, calculations, and orchestrating calls to repositories. That logic is pure Java and doesn't need Spring context or a database to verify. I'd use the Mockito extension to mock the repository and inject it into the service, then write tests that verify the logic itself. For example, if I have an order service that applies discounts based on customer tier, I'd mock the repository to return a test order, call the discount method, and assert the result is correct. This runs in milliseconds because there's no context startup. Integration tests are only needed when you're testing real database queries—like a custom JPQL method—or verifying that multiple Spring beans wire together correctly. A common mistake freshers make is adding the SpringBootTest annotation to every service test, which loads the entire application context and makes the test suite incredibly slow. The rule of thumb is: if you're testing logic, use a unit test with mocks. If you're testing wiring or real database behaviour, use an integration test. That keeps your test suite fast and focused.

questions.question: What is a test slice in Spring Boot and why is it useful?
questions.title: What Are Test Slices
questions.direct_answer: A **test slice** is a Spring Boot auto-configuration that loads only **one layer** of the application — like web or JPA — instead of the full context, making tests faster and more focused. Examples include **@WebMvcTest** for controllers and **@DataJpaTest** for repositories.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Spring Boot's built-in test infrastructure beyond @SpringBootTest and knowing when to use slices.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for everything, not knowing slice annotations exist, and ending up with unnecessarily slow tests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name multiple slices—@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest—and explain what each loads and when to use it.

sections.title: Test Slices for Focused Layer Testing
sections.content:
**Test slices** are Spring Boot annotations that load only a **subset of your application context**—the beans and auto-configurations needed for a specific layer. Instead of starting the entire application with @SpringBootTest, you use a slice annotation to test just the web layer, just the JPA layer, or just JSON serialization.

Think of it like ordering a slice of pizza instead of the whole pie: you get exactly what you need, faster and cheaper. **@WebMvcTest** loads only Spring MVC infrastructure for controller tests. **@DataJpaTest** loads only JPA repositories, an in-memory database, and transaction management. **@JsonTest** loads just Jackson for testing JSON serialization. This approach makes tests **10-50x faster** because Spring doesn't scan for unrelated beans, doesn't read unused configuration, and doesn't connect to external systems you're not testing.

sections.title: Common Slices at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|@WebMvcTest|~Web layer only|Spring MVC plus MockMvc|mock services with @MockBean|controller tests
emerald|@DataJpaTest|~JPA layer only|repositories plus H2|rolls back per test|query tests
amber|@JsonTest|~Jackson only|serialize and deserialize|no app beans|DTO tests
rose|Why slices|~Load less, run faster|1-3s versus 10-30s|focused failures|cached per slice

sections.title: Using @WebMvcTest to Test a Controller
When to Use Each Slice
sections.content:
Use **@WebMvcTest** when testing REST controllers to verify request mappings, validation, HTTP status codes, and JSON responses without loading the service or database layers.

Use **@DataJpaTest** when testing custom repository methods or complex JPQL queries to ensure they return the correct data from a real database—it auto-configures an in-memory H2 database and rolls back transactions after each test.

Use **@JsonTest** when you need to verify that your DTOs serialize/deserialize correctly with Jackson, especially for custom date formats or field naming strategies.

Use **@RestClientTest** when testing a component that makes HTTP calls to external APIs, mocking the RestTemplate or WebClient.

Use **@SpringBootTest** only when you need to test how multiple layers work together in a real end-to-end scenario.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing slices exist**: Freshers learn @SpringBootTest first and use it everywhere, never discovering that Spring Boot provides faster, layer-specific alternatives. This makes the test suite painfully slow as it grows.
- **Mixing slice annotations**: Adding @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest to the same test class, which causes conflicts because each slice configures its own limited context. You can't test a controller and a repository in the same slice—they belong to different layers.
- **Not using @MockBean**: Forgetting that slice tests don't load your service beans, then getting NoSuchBeanDefinitionException errors because the controller's dependency isn't available.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Test slice** — a Spring Boot annotation that loads only the beans and config needed for one layer.
- **@WebMvcTest** — loads Spring MVC, MockMvc, and the specified controller; no services or repositories.
- **@DataJpaTest** — loads JPA repositories, an in-memory H2 database, and transaction support; no web layer.
- **@JsonTest** — loads the Jackson ObjectMapper for JSON serialization tests, no application beans.
- **@MockBean requirement** — slices don't load dependencies, so mock them with @MockBean in the test class.
- **Speed improvement** — slice tests start in 1-3 seconds versus 10-30 seconds for @SpringBootTest.
- **Context caching** — Spring caches slice contexts, so later tests using the same slice reuse the context.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A test slice is a Spring Boot annotation that loads only part of your application context instead of the whole thing. It's designed to test one specific layer in isolation. For example, the WebMvcTest annotation loads just the web layer—Spring MVC, the controller you specify, and MockMvc for simulating HTTP requests. It doesn't load your services or repositories, so you have to mock them with the MockBean annotation. This makes the test way faster because Spring isn't scanning your entire application or connecting to databases. Another example is the DataJpaTest annotation, which loads only JPA repositories and an in-memory database. You'd use this to test a custom repository method that has a JPQL query. Spring Boot provides slices for different layers: JsonTest for testing JSON serialization, RestClientTest for testing HTTP client code, and several others. The key benefit is speed and focus. A slice test might start in two seconds, while a full-context test takes fifteen seconds. A common mistake freshers make is not knowing these exist, so they use the SpringBootTest annotation for everything and wonder why their test suite takes forever to run. Once you understand slices, you can test each layer appropriately without the overhead of a full context.

questions.question: What happens when you annotate a test with @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: What @SpringBootTest Does
questions.direct_answer: **@SpringBootTest** triggers Spring Boot's **full application context startup** — it scans for components, reads configuration files, connects to databases, and wires every dependency, exactly as if the app were running normally. That power is why it's slow and reserved for integration tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of what @SpringBootTest actually does under the hood and the cost it incurs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that it starts a full context, including database connections and configuration loading, treating it as lightweight.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention webEnvironment parameter options—MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT, NONE—and context caching between tests.

sections.title: Full Application Context Startup
sections.content:
When you annotate a test class with **@SpringBootTest**, Spring Boot performs the exact same startup sequence it does when you run your application normally. It **scans for @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller** classes in the base package and subpackages. It **loads application.properties or application.yml** to configure beans. It triggers **auto-configuration** for JPA, web servers, security, and any other starters you have. It **connects to databases** if DataSource beans are configured. It **wires all dependencies** through dependency injection.

Think of it as booting your entire application inside the test—every bean gets created, every connection gets established, every configuration gets applied. This is powerful for **end-to-end integration tests** but extremely expensive for simple unit tests. A @SpringBootTest can take 10-30 seconds to start, compared to milliseconds for a pure unit test.

sections.title: What @SpringBootTest Sets in Motion
sections.content:
emerald|What it does|~Boots the full app|scans components|reads application.yml|auto-configures everything
blue|webEnvironment|~Controls the web layer|MOCK is default|RANDOM_PORT real server|NONE no web
amber|The cost|~Slow startup|10-30s for medium apps|context is cached|reuse if config matches
rose|Use it for|~True integration|cross-layer flows|critical happy paths|not isolated logic

sections.title: Using @SpringBootTest for an End-to-End Test
When to Use @SpringBootTest
sections.content: Use **@SpringBootTest** when you need to verify that multiple layers of your application work together correctly in a realistic scenario. Examples: testing that a REST endpoint correctly processes a request, calls the service, persists to the database, and returns the expected HTTP response. Testing that scheduled jobs execute with the correct transaction behavior. Testing that security filters and authentication work as configured. Testing that message listeners consume from a queue and update the database. Do NOT use @SpringBootTest for testing a single service method's business logic or a single controller's request mapping—those should use unit tests or slice tests instead. Reserve @SpringBootTest for **critical happy paths** and **complex cross-layer flows** that you can't validate any other way.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for everything**: Freshers add it to every test class because it's the first annotation they learn, not realizing it makes tests 50-100x slower and doesn't provide better coverage for isolated logic.
- **Not understanding webEnvironment options**: Using the default MOCK environment when testing REST endpoints, then getting confused why TestRestTemplate doesn't work—you need RANDOM_PORT for real HTTP calls.
- **Ignoring context startup time**: Not noticing that tests take 15 seconds to start, assuming that's normal, and never learning about slice annotations or unit tests that run in milliseconds.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Full context startup** — loads all beans, runs auto-configuration, connects to databases, reads config files.
- **webEnvironment.MOCK** — the default; starts the context without a real HTTP server; use with MockMvc.
- **webEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT** — starts a real embedded server on a random port; use with TestRestTemplate.
- **webEnvironment.DEFINED_PORT** — starts the server on the configured port; rarely used in tests.
- **webEnvironment.NONE** — loads the context with no web environment; for background jobs.
- **Context caching** — Spring caches contexts between classes when configurations are identical.
- **Startup cost** — typically 10-30 seconds for medium apps, unsuitable for fast feedback unit tests.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you annotate a test with the SpringBootTest annotation, Spring Boot starts the full application context just like it does when you run the application normally. It scans for all your components, services, repositories, and controllers. It reads your application properties file and applies all the auto-configuration for JPA, web servers, security, and any other Spring Boot starters you have. It connects to your database if you have a data source configured. It wires all the dependencies together through dependency injection. Essentially, it boots your entire application inside the test environment. You can control the web environment with a parameter. The default is MOCK, which loads the context without starting a real server—you use MockMvc here. If you set it to RANDOM_PORT, Spring starts an embedded Tomcat on a random port, and you can use TestRestTemplate to make real HTTP requests. There's also NONE for tests that don't need any web layer, like testing scheduled jobs. One thing to know is that this annotation is slow—it can take ten to thirty seconds to start. Spring does cache the context, so if multiple test classes use the same configuration, they'll reuse the same context. A common mistake freshers make is using it for simple service tests where a unit test would be much faster and just as effective. You should reserve it for true integration tests that verify multiple layers working together.

questions.question: Can a Spring Boot test be both a unit test and use Spring annotations at the same time?
questions.title: Mixing Unit and Spring Annotations
questions.direct_answer: **No** — a true unit test doesn't load a Spring context, so mixing Spring annotations turns it into an integration test and adds overhead without benefit. Use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** for unit tests; any Spring annotation like @SpringBootTest or @Autowired signals an integration test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has clear conceptual boundaries between test types and doesn't blur the lines.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @SpringBootTest to tests that only test a service method, treating all tests as integration tests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) is the correct choice for unit tests and doesn't involve Spring at all—it's pure JUnit 5 and Mockito.

sections.title: Clear Boundaries Between Test Types
sections.content:
A **unit test** tests a single class in complete isolation from external systems—no databases, no HTTP servers, no dependency injection frameworks. You manually instantiate the class under test and provide mocked dependencies through constructor injection or setters.

The key characteristic is that **no Spring context is loaded**. If you add Spring annotations like @SpringBootTest, @Autowired, or @MockBean, you're no longer writing a unit test—you've crossed into **integration test** territory where Spring manages beans and wiring.

Think of it like this: unit tests are pure Java, integration tests involve frameworks. The moment you involve Spring's dependency injection, you're testing not just your logic but also how Spring wires things together. For true unit tests, use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** from JUnit 5, which activates Mockito without loading any application context. This keeps tests **blazingly fast** and focused on logic alone.

sections.title: Where the Line Is Drawn
sections.content:
emerald|Unit test|~Pure Java plus Mockito|@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension)|@Mock and @InjectMocks|no context loaded
rose|The moment you add|~Spring annotations|@SpringBootTest|@Autowired or @MockBean|it's now integration
amber|@Mock vs @MockBean|~Easy to confuse|@Mock is Mockito, unit|@MockBean is Spring, integration|pick by context
blue|Rule of thumb|~No context needed?|then it's a unit test|frameworks mean integration|keep the line clear

sections.title: True Unit Test Without Spring
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** for testing service layer business logic, utility classes, validators, and any code that doesn't require Spring's dependency injection to function. These tests run in milliseconds and give instant feedback when logic breaks. Examples: testing discount calculation, input validation, data transformation, algorithm implementation.

Use **Spring test annotations** like @SpringBootTest or @DataJpaTest when you need to verify that components integrate correctly through Spring's wiring, that transactions behave correctly, or that custom repository queries return the right data. Examples: testing that @Transactional rollback works, that a REST endpoint processes requests correctly, that a scheduled job executes with proper context. If your test can work without starting a Spring context, it should be a unit test.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding @SpringBootTest to service tests**: Freshers think they need Spring to test a service class, so they add @SpringBootTest and @Autowired, making a simple logic test take 15 seconds to start. The service doesn't need Spring to run—it's just a Java class with dependencies.
- **Using @MockBean in unit tests**: Mixing Mockito's @Mock with Spring's @MockBean, not understanding that @MockBean requires a Spring context to replace a bean. Unit tests use @Mock, integration tests use @MockBean.
- **Not understanding the definition**: Thinking that any test using JUnit is a unit test, regardless of what framework layers it involves.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unit test definition** — tests a single class in isolation with mocked dependencies, no frameworks involved.
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** — activates Mockito for JUnit 5 tests without loading any Spring context.
- **@Mock vs @MockBean** — @Mock is Mockito's annotation for unit tests; @MockBean is Spring's for integration tests.
- **@InjectMocks** — a Mockito annotation that creates an instance and injects mocks into it, with no Spring involvement.
- **Spring annotations = integration test** — any test using @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, or @Autowired is integration.
- **Speed difference** — unit tests run in milliseconds; Spring integration tests take seconds due to context startup.
- **Conceptual clarity** — if you're loading a framework to run your test, it's not a unit test by definition.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: No, a test can't be both a unit test and use Spring annotations at the same time. By definition, a unit test tests a single class in complete isolation without loading any frameworks or external systems. The moment you add Spring annotations like SpringBootTest or Autowired, you're loading the Spring application context, which makes it an integration test. For true unit tests, you use the ExtendWith annotation with MockitoExtension from JUnit 5. That activates Mockito so you can use the Mock annotation to create mock objects and the InjectMocks annotation to inject them into the class you're testing. No Spring is involved at all—it's pure Java and Mockito. For example, if I'm testing a payment service that depends on a payment gateway and a repository, I'd mock those two dependencies with Mockito and inject them into the service. The test runs in milliseconds because there's no context startup, no bean scanning, no configuration loading. A common mistake freshers make is adding the SpringBootTest annotation to service tests because they think they need Spring to test a service class. But the service is just a Java class—you don't need Spring's dependency injection to instantiate it and call its methods. Using Spring annotations when you don't need them makes tests slow and blurs the line between unit and integration testing. If your test can work without a Spring context, it should be a unit test with Mockito.
